notes: Reinsurance claims control clause appeal; construction of preliminary issues and follow-the-settlements interaction is fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Reinsurance claims control clause and follow settlements
key_facts: Eagle Star settled Varian's environmental pollution claim for US$1 million plus costs without reinsurers controlling negotiations or settlement.
Lloyd's and company reinsurers on a 1970 umbrella excess policy relied on a typed claims co-operation/control clause requiring underwriter control of negotiations and settlement.
Morison J held sub-paragraph (b) was not a condition precedent and that reinsurers remained bound to follow Eagle Star's settlement.
Reinsurers had received broker advices from 1990 to 1992 but did not control the 1995 Varian settlement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from preliminary issues on construction of a modified claims co-operation clause in reinsurance policies.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; control of negotiations or settlement is a condition precedent to liability unless waiver or other excuse applies; reinsurers need not follow settlements not controlled or consented to.
enrichment.ratio: Sub-paragraph (b) allocates reinsurers a controlling role over negotiations and settlements; where negotiations or settlement occur without that control, the clause excludes liability to pay the claim; typed clauses limiting settlement without consent and omitting follow-the-settlements language override the printed J1 form obligation.
legal_issues: Whether sub-paragraph (b) imposes an option or allocates a controlling role to reinsurers
Whether compliance with the claims control clause is a condition precedent to indemnity
Whether the follow the settlements clause survives the typed policy attachments
Meaning of limits stated in the schedule in the apportionment of costs clause

notes: Exclusive supply contract and implied terms appeal; judge's eight-month delay criticised but implied-term and delivery conclusions are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Exclusive supply contract: implied terms and goods delivery
key_facts: TRS agreed in August 1999 to buy all conservatory roofing requirements exclusively from Ultraframe in return for increased discounts.
Ultraframe allegedly ran a campaign in 2000 to divert TRS customers to deal direct; TRS accepted alleged repudiatory breach in September 2000.
The judge held implied restrictions on Ultraframe's competition could not be implied and that disputed goods worth £21,328.92 had been delivered.
The trial judge took eight months to deliver judgment after a hearing ending in October 2002.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission on implied terms and delivery of goods issues after reserved judgment in a repudiatory breach dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on both issues; implied good-faith/non-injury terms rejected and delivery finding upheld without retrial.
enrichment.ratio: No term can be implied preventing Ultraframe from lawfully soliciting TRS customers where the contract expressly required exclusive purchasing but did not restrict the supplier's freedom to compete or fix prices; on the evidence TRS's delayed and undifferentiated response supported a finding that all despatch-note goods were delivered.
legal_issues: Whether terms restraining deliberate customer poaching or requiring good faith should be implied
Application of BP Refinery and Philips v BSkyB implied-term conditions to exclusive supply agreements
Whether factual findings on partial delivery should be retried given judge's delay

notes: Council tax sole or main residence appeal; Williams v Horsham applied straightforwardly where owner never lived at the dwelling.

enrichment.short_title: Council tax where owner never resided at dwelling
key_facts: Mr Bennett owned Woodville Cottage in Cumbria but lived a nomadic life in Bedfordshire and elsewhere for work, visiting the property only occasionally.
The valuation tribunal held the Cumbria property was his sole or main residence because he had no other property with a financial interest.
The deputy judge upheld the tribunal, treating non-residence as only one factor among ownership, right to return, and retirement intention.
Williams v Horsham District Council held sole or main residence requires premises in which the taxpayer actually resides.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from deputy High Court judge upholding a valuation tribunal council tax liability decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Woodville Cottage was not Mr Bennett's sole or main residence and he was not a resident for section 6 purposes.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 6(5) of the 1992 Act a person cannot be a resident of a dwelling in which he has never lived; where no actual residence exists at the owned property, ownership and intention to retire there do not convert it into sole or main residence.
legal_issues: Meaning of resident and sole or main residence under section 6(5)
Effect of Williams v Horsham on earlier council tax residence authorities
Whether ownership without occupation suffices for council tax liability as a resident freeholder

notes: Unopposed judicial review quashing speed-limit convictions after missing traffic order; Scally principles applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Quashing speed convictions for invalid 30 mph limit
key_facts: Mr Pownall and Mr Rodber pleaded guilty to exceeding 30 mph on the B5441 Welsh Road in Sealand in 2001 and 2002.
The requisite traffic order supporting the 30 mph limit was later found absent, so the legal limit was 60 mph and neither was speeding.
Police solicitors confirmed the offences would be withdrawn and suggested judicial review after guilty pleas precluded Crown Court appeal.
A similar unopposed claim in R (Smith) v Flintshire Magistrates Court had already resulted in quashing the conviction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Unopposed judicial review claims to quash magistrates' court convictions entered on guilty pleas.
enrichment.outcome: Both convictions quashed; North Wales Police ordered to pay each claimant's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where convictions rest on flawed prosecution evidence that denied defendants a proper choice whether to plead guilty, judicial review may quash convictions even without court unfairness or prosecutorial dishonesty, analogously to R v Bolton justices ex parte Scally.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review lies to quash convictions after guilty pleas
Application of ex parte Scally where the legal speed limit was misstated
Appropriate remedy when section 142 Magistrates' Courts Act does not apply
linked_authorities: R v Bolton Justices ex parte Scally [1991] 2 All ER 619
R (Smith) v Flintshire Magistrates Court [2003] EWCA 106 (Admin)

notes: Substantial ancillary relief judgment on offshore trusts and Lewis's special needs; dispositive order terms appear at end of findings but full minute of order is not in the extracted text.

enrichment.short_title: Ancillary relief with offshore trusts and special-needs child
key_facts: The parties married in 1997 after cohabitation from 1995 and have a son Lewis with complex developmental and behavioural difficulties.
Nearly all wealth is held in offshore H family trusts, principally the Husband's Fund worth about £6.4 million gross.
The Wife sought substantial provision including housing; legal costs exceeded £400,000 between the parties.
The judge ordered a life-interest housing trust of about £575,000, a £55,000 lump sum, and £40,000 annual maintenance plus urgent therapeutic funding for Lewis from the Grandchildren's Settlement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Final hearing of Wife's application for full ancillary relief after acrimonious contested disclosure on trust assets.
enrichment.outcome: Wife awarded life-interest housing fund, lump sum, indexed maintenance, and Lewis's therapeutic and mediation costs to be funded from family trusts with judicious encouragement to trustees under Thomas v Thomas.
enrichment.ratio: Where matrimonial resources derive from family trusts, fairness is measured by needs and the husband's ability to pay through trustee cooperation rather than equal sharing; the court may frame orders to encourage trustees where other beneficiaries would not be appreciably harmed and release is reasonably likely.
legal_issues: Appropriate financial provision from offshore discretionary and life-interest trusts
Application of Thomas v Thomas and judicious encouragement of trustees
Quantification of housing and income needs given Lewis's special needs
Tax-efficient borrowing from the Husband's Fund to meet awards and costs

notes: Combined anonymised care appeals with extensive Cannings guidance; two separate threshold outcomes and reporting restrictions limit public detail.

enrichment.short_title: Care proceedings after Cannings: standard of proof
key_facts: Two anonymised appeals raised the civil standard of proof and the impact of R v Cannings on care threshold findings.
In LU, Bracewell J found the mother caused deliberate airway obstruction incidents; permission to appeal and extension of time were refused.
In LB, the mother was found responsible for rigor episodes; permission and extension were granted but the appeal was dismissed.
The court held Cannings does not alter local authorities' Children Act duties or replace the re H balance-of-probability approach.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Combined Court of Appeal judgment on permission and substantive appeals from section 31 threshold findings in two care cases.
enrichment.outcome: Cannings guidance affirmed for family proceedings; LU appeal refused at permission stage; LB appeal dismissed on merits.
enrichment.ratio: The standard of proof in care proceedings remains the balance of probabilities per re H, not the criminal standard; Cannings warns against over-dogmatic medical conclusions but does not require local authorities to abandon proceedings wherever experts disagree if clear extraneous evidence supports harm attributable to parental conduct.
legal_issues: Correct standard of proof after McCann and B v Chief Constable of Avon and Somerset
Impact of R v Cannings on section 31 threshold findings
Use of non-medical and contextual evidence where medical experts disagree
Whether expert disagreement alone bars care proceedings

notes: ASBO evidential time limit issue resolved clearly; out-of-time conduct admissible for necessity evaluation under section 1(1)(b).

enrichment.short_title: ASBO evidence outside six-month complaint limit
key_facts: Ryan Stevens challenged an ASBO made by South East Surrey Magistrates on 16 September 2003.
Police relied on 30 alleged incidents, only eight within six months of the complaint, to show necessity under section 1(1)(b).
Magistrates proved eight in-time incidents to the criminal standard and considered older hearsay incidents when evaluating necessity.
The claimant argued section 127 barred proof of the 22 out-of-time incidents.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review following grant of permission to challenge an anti-social behaviour order.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; magistrates were entitled to admit out-of-time conduct evidence when assessing necessity for the ASBO.
enrichment.ratio: Section 127 governs jurisdiction to entertain a complaint, not admissibility once jurisdiction exists over recent acts; evidence of earlier anti-social behaviour may properly inform the evaluative necessity inquiry under section 1(1)(b), subject to relevance, fairness, and weight.
legal_issues: Whether section 127 prevents reliance on out-of-time anti-social behaviour in ASBO applications
Distinction between proof of anti-social acts under section 1(1)(a) and necessity under section 1(1)(b)
Admissibility and weight of hearsay evidence in ASBO proceedings after McCann

notes: Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal striking-off appeal; Bolton principles applied with no interference warranted.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor struck off for accounts breaches and obstruction
key_facts: Duncan James Kidd, sole principal of Kidd & Co, was struck off on 18 June 2003 for serious Solicitors Accounts Rules breaches.
He failed to reconcile client accounts, filed no Accountant's Reports, obstructed OSS inspections, and misled investigators about records being up to date.
Law Society intervention required a Chancery court order before access to books was obtained.
The solicitor had a previously unblemished 20-year career but deliberately frustrated regulatory oversight over a lengthy period.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 55 Solicitors Act 1974 against Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal striking-off decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs summarily assessed at £2,945.94 payable in two months.
enrichment.ratio: Persistent failure to maintain client accounting records, false assurances to the regulator, and deliberate obstruction of investigation fall so far below standards of integrity, probity, and trustworthiness that striking off remains appropriate despite personal mitigation and absence of client dishonesty.
legal_issues: Appropriate sanction for Solicitors Accounts Rules breaches without misappropriation
Whether misleading the OSS is less serious than misleading clients
Appellate deference to the Tribunal under Bolton v Law Society

notes: Complex VAT reinsurance repair scheme; three issues resolved with split outcomes for Commissioners, WHA, and Viscount.

enrichment.short_title: VAT on motor breakdown insurance repair scheme

statutes_considered.title: Sixth Council Directive 77/388/EEC on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to turnover taxes
Council Directive 86/560/EEC on the harmonization of the laws of the Member States relating to turnover taxes

key_facts: A group VAT scheme minimised liability on motor breakdown insurance repairs through Gibraltar reinsurer Viscount and claims handler WHA.
Garages invoiced WHA with VAT; WHA invoiced Viscount contending its services were exempt, seeking recovery of input tax from Customs and Excise.
The VAT and Duties Tribunal upheld the Commissioners on all three central issues; Lloyd J allowed WHA's appeal in part.
The Court of Appeal held garages supplied WHA, WHA's supply to Viscount was taxable, but Viscount could recover that VAT as input tax.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by Customs and Excise from Lloyd J's decision allowing part of WHA and Viscount's appeal from the VAT and Duties Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Commissioners succeeded against WHA on taxability of its invoice to Viscount but must refund VAT paid by Viscount to WHA; garage-to-WHA supply upheld.
enrichment.ratio: There is a supply of repair services by garages to WHA enabling WHA's input tax recovery in principle; WHA makes a taxable supply to Viscount rather than an exempt insurance-related supply; Viscount as a person carrying on business in the Community may recover that VAT as input tax under domestic and Sixth Directive provisions.
legal_issues: Whether garage repairs are supplied to WHA or directly to the policyholder
Whether WHA's claims-handling charges to Viscount are taxable or exempt
Whether Viscount may recover VAT charged by WHA as input tax

notes: Narrow planning injunction appeal; partial amendment on vehicle movement wording and Moor Lane scope.

enrichment.short_title: Planning injunction scope at Poyle Place lorry park
key_facts: Slough Borough Council obtained an injunction restraining commercial vehicle parking and portable buildings at Poyle Place, Horton Road.
Mr Prashar appealed limited permission points on northern Moor Lane inclusion and prohibition of cross-land vehicle movement to Spelthorne land.
The deputy judge found continued lorry-park use despite enforcement notices and encroachment beyond noticed areas.
Mediation was requested but the court declined adjournment and partially amended the order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with limited permission against Queen's Bench planning injunction order of 2 December 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal partly allowed: movement wording amended to permit access-related movement but not general transit storage; Moor Lane scope appeal dismissed with plan clarified.
enrichment.ratio: An section 187B injunction need not be confined to land covered by enforcement notices where evidence shows breach beyond those areas; prohibitions on movement should not block lawful access across council land to adjoining sites outside the council's planning control.
legal_issues: Whether injunction land must match enforcement notice boundaries
Proper drafting of restrictions on movement versus parking and storage of commercial vehicles
Interaction between Slough and Spelthorne planning jurisdictions
